Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Palais Lascaris, Nice, France - Museum Tour
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2655

Orientation: You are about to explore the Palais Lascaris in Nice, a museum showcasing a selection of exquisite musical instruments from the Renaissance to the Enlightenment. These works embody the evolution of musical craftsmanship, each resonating with the ingenuity and artistry of its respective era. Your first stop is Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652). As you stand before the Violes gambe by William Turner, crafted in 1652, notice its strikingly preserved structure. From this vantage point, you can appreciate the craftsmanship of this six-string bass viola da gamba. The detailing in its construction, featuring a bent front of Baltic pine or fir staves, becomes evident. This choice of materials was typical of Turner's work in his London workshop.

 He bequeathed an extensive collection of musical instruments to the city, and in 1904, this collection, including Turner's Violes gambe, became part of the Palais Lascaris. This ensured the viol was preserved in substantially its original condition. William Turner, an English luthier primarily recognized for his painting, crafted this instrument during a time when viols were central to musical ensembles in English courts, subtly intertwining music and politics. His construction technique, emphasizing the use of fine woods and intricate purfling, not only ensured a rich tonal quality but also extended the instrument's durability. Unlike many viols of its era, which were often transformed into violoncellos in subsequent centuries, this particular piece has remained largely untouched. The instrument's presence in this collection, alongside others like the recorder by Denner and violins by Gagliano and Schorn, showcases a fascinating narrative of musical evolution. The Palais Lascaris, recognized as the second most important collection of historical instruments in France, illustrates the diverse contributions to music from different European regions. This viol, along with others in the collection, offers a glimpse into the intricate world of seventeenth-century music, where craftsmanship and sound converged to create instruments that resonated through time.

Directions: Continue through Palais Lascaris — next is Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780).

Stop 2: Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2655

Orientation: Stand a few steps back from the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) to appreciate its full height of 161.5 centimeters. This distance allows you to see the elegant curvature of the instrument and the intricate craftsmanship that marks it as a quintessential piece of 18th-century French artistry.

In 2007, the city of Nice acquired this remarkable harp crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman, dated 1780. It was discovered preserved in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. As a result, the harp became part of the musical instrument collection at Palais Lascaris, where it now carries the museum inventory number PL.2007.9.1, contributing to the rich cultural tapestry of the museum's offerings. The Harpe by Naderman is constructed from wood and various materials, showcasing a single-action pedal mechanism that utilizes crochets, or hooks, to raise the pitch of the strings by a semitone. This technological decision was innovative at the time, allowing musicians a greater range of expression and playing flexibility. Its design reflects the broader cultural shift in 18th-century France, where music increasingly became a form of personal expression and an emblem of burgeoning bourgeois culture. Historically, this harp once belonged to the Viscountess of Beaumont, signifying its connection to the French aristocracy. The label inside the neck reads: 'NADERMAN / Mtre. Luthier Facteur de Harpe ordinaire / du service de la Reine / Rue d'Argenteuil Butte / St. Roch à Paris 1780', indicating its prestigious origins and the maker’s royal affiliation. From the viols you saw earlier, which laid the groundwork for stringed instruments in Europe, to this harp, it's evident how musical instruments evolved to embody personal and cultural expression.

Directions: Next: Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581).

Stop 3: Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2655

Orientation: As you stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, pause to admire the craftsmanship from a vantage point where the engraved decorative garland on the bell is clearly visible. This position offers an appreciation of the delicate engravings and the instrument's historical markings, grounding you in the era it heralds from.

Before 2001, the Sacqueboute ténor crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581 resided in various institutions across Nice, including the Musée des Beaux-Arts and the Musée Masséna, before finding a temporary home at the Conservatoire de Nice. Schnitzer, renowned for his craftsmanship in Nuremberg's bustling environment for brass instrument creation, produced this distinctive instrument with a U-shaped slide and two parallel sliding tubes—a characteristic design of early trombones. This design allowed for greater versatility in pitch and volume, making it instrumental in the grand ceremonies of the Holy Roman Empire, where such instruments were used to fill vast spaces with their commanding sound. Fischer later highlighted this particular sackbut in the Historic Brass Society Journal, underscoring its significance as one of the earliest surviving sackbuts in original condition. Notably, the Sacqueboute ténor retains its original mouthpiece, a rarity among surviving sixteenth-century trombones, which offers modern scholars and musicians insight into the soundscapes of the late Renaissance. As you reflect on Schnitzer's work, recalling the detailed craftsmanship of the harp you admired earlier in this tour, consider how these historical instruments collectively tell the story of their time—each one not only a piece of art but a witness to the rich cultural tapestries they once enriched.

Directions: Your final stop in Palais Lascaris: Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696).

Stop 4: Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2655

Orientation: Stand to the left of Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, observing the instrument's elegant curves and craftsmanship, reminiscent of the rich musical history of the Palais Lascaris's current home.

Initially, it was kept in -Arts de Nice and later moved to the Musée Masséna, illustrating the fluidity of cultural assets in the city. Paolo Antonio Testore hailed from a family deeply rooted in the tradition of instrument making. His father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore, founded the Testore workshop in Milan, having learned the art. Paolo, along with his brother Carlo Antonio, maintained their father's legacy, with Paolo specializing in crafting instruments that combined robust design with exceptional acoustics. This Basse de violon embodies the craftsmanship for which the Testore family became renowned. The dark varnish and detailed curves not only showcase its aesthetic appeal but also contribute to its rich, full-bodied sound, setting it apart from other instruments of its time.

That's 4 stops — Sacqueboute ténor with original mouthpiece, crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581 and Violes gambe crafted by William Turner in 1652, now at Palais Lascaris.
